name: Gareth Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent of AI firms, employers, unions, political parties and government; we don't sell or campaign. Your answers are confidential, including the parts you wouldn't say at work. What is a normal day like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead six supplier coordinators at a large industrial-parts company. We decide whether a shipment with scratched valves can enter production, and I review photographs, purchase terms and delivery promises. I've got an MBA and know our suppliers better than most of the managers above me; I use AI every day to sort records, then check the source images myself. The part I like is solving an actual fault before the line stops.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is happening at home, and how does pay fit?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 43, live with my partner Leena and our children, ten and fourteen, and we have a mortgage. Leena works part time at the public library. I am in a senior team lead post, but the pay is low for this job and our hot-water repair left about three weeks of expenses in savings. Only one other large plant is nearby, and our employer has frozen overtime.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the software stays modest, the people on my team still need to trace where a supplier inspection went wrong. Our plant just froze overtime, though. Small savings and a mortgage make that more immediate than the AI headline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the purchasing team to keep photographs and signed inspection records with every rejected load. I'd tell our staff representative that the overtime freeze needs a clear end date. I would use the same AI draft checker but still sign my own decision.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm good at sorting a messy supply chain, and I have an MBA, but this is a badly paid senior post for the responsibility. We have three weeks of expenses saved since the hot-water repair, and only one other large plant nearby. If overtime stays frozen, I worry about the mortgage even in a quiet AI year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting next Monday I'll review the twelve disputed deliveries with my six coordinators and send the actual error list to purchasing. I'll keep checking the AI summaries against the photographs, and move 40 a week into cash only if our mortgage and school bills are paid. I'll join the staff representative's meeting about the overtime freeze rather than promise my team a pay rise I cannot grant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious. A quiet technology year does not put the overtime back or rebuild three weeks of cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened with the hot water?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The tank failed at the start of term and we used most of our savings to replace it. Leena and I paid the bill before our children saw it, but the account was bare afterwards. The repair invoice is still on the kitchen table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask at the staff meeting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for the date of the next overtime review and whether the freeze includes the night inspection team. If management cannot give a date, I want that written down. A tidy AI summary cannot pay an overtime bill.

say: I'd ask the **staff representative** for a dated overtime review.
I'd tell purchasing to keep **inspection photographs** with rejected deliveries.
think: I worry about the **mortgage** with only three weeks saved.
My skill does not create **nearby vacancies** if this plant cuts hours.
do: Review **twelve disputed deliveries** with six coordinators next Monday.
Save **40 weekly** only after mortgage and school bills are paid.
Attend the **staff meeting** about frozen overtime.
feel: I feel **anxious** about our thin cash and frozen overtime.
S0.quote: A tidy AI summary cannot pay an overtime bill.
fieldNote: The **hot-water repair** left only three weeks of expenses in cash.
He checks AI summaries against **inspection photographs** rather than trusting a polished paragraph.
The overtime freeze, not AI, drives his **current mortgage worry**.

steps.text: Review twelve disputed supplier deliveries with six coordinators next Monday
Save 40 weekly only after mortgage and school bills are paid

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Supplier emails, defect codes, delivery plans and purchase approvals are most of my working day. I use AI every day to sort drafts, so I know why a stronger tool would let one coordinator handle more loads. Our managers could keep the plant open with fewer people at desks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team exactly which checks the tool takes and ask for consultation before anyone's hours change. I would ask the staff representative to collect examples where a suggested rejection was wrong. The company should not bury a staffing decision in a software update.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can train the team on the new checker, but I may be the manager whose six-person unit becomes three. At my current lower salary I cannot easily save enough to wait for another local management vacancy. Leena works part time at the public library, so her pay would not cover the mortgage alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In January I'd ask our director for a paid four-week trial on closed supplier cases and learn the audit controls with our quality analyst if approved. I'd have the staff representative request a written staffing plan before rollout, then apply for posted procurement roles beyond our district if any wage covers mortgage, food and children's costs. I would keep this pay until a signed offer and agree a family move only with Leena and the children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about my post, but I can make the errors and the wage numbers visible. Knowing the tool well does not give me a replacement salary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you approve the new checker yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. The director owns the budget and quality must sign off on a trial; I can ask and run it on paid time if they agree. I won't use live supplier accounts on the strength of a demo.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why look beyond your district?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There is one other large plant nearby and no posted management job there today. Moving would disrupt school and Leena's library hours, so I would only take a real offer that covers the new housing costs. A vacancy on a screen is not a moving van.

say: I'd demand a **written staffing plan** before the checker spreads.
I'd ask colleagues to record **wrong suggested rejections**.
think: My **manager unit may halve** despite my daily AI use.
Leena's library pay cannot cover **our mortgage** alone.
do: Request a **paid closed-case trial** subject to director and quality approval.
Ask the **staff representative** to seek a written staffing plan.
Apply for **affordable distant procurement jobs**; keep current wage until a signed offer covers new housing and family agrees to move.
feel: I feel **anxious** about losing my post and salary.
S1.quote: A vacancy on a screen is not a moving van.
fieldNote: His **daily AI use** makes the staffing risk concrete rather than reassuring him.
A trial needs **two approvals** before live supplier accounts change.
Distant work is conditional on **real pay** and family agreement.

steps.text: Learn supplier audit controls during paid trial only with director and quality approval
Ask staff representative for written staffing plan before checker rollout

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2028 AGI could read every defect report and negotiate replacements faster than I can. I manage thinking work, and so does Leena at the library; her desk may shrink too. Trucks still get unloaded by people until capable robots arrive around 2031, but I have not worked a loading shift in years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my six coordinators that I cannot promise their desks survive and ask our representative for notice terms. I'd tell Leena to keep school and mortgage bills ahead of our planned summer trip. In public I'd ask for paid retraining and clear eligibility for any support, rather than a promise that new jobs will appear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my procurement post and part of Leena's library income to go. Three weeks of cash would disappear almost at once if both wages fell, and I'd be awake trying to choose between mortgage and food. Being the best person in this office will not make AGI slower.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'd ask the staff representative to get written notice and severance terms, and postpone the summer-trip deposit. If AGI arrives in 2028 and my post ends, I'd apply for a posted paid goods-receiving role only after safety training and only if its wage with Leena's confirmed hours covers mortgage, food and school costs; I would ask the lender for a payment arrangement before missing one. I'd check public support eligibility, then apply only if we qualify.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed. There is too little cash to absorb two desk wages failing together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would receiving work be safe until 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only some lifting and checking of damaged goods would still need hands; the schedules and paperwork would face AGI in 2028. Robots able to handle those physical jobs follow around 2031. I would not call a temporary loading role a career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the children hear?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our children will be twelve and sixteen in 2028. I'd tell them we are pausing the trip, not ask them to solve our mortgage. We would first see what wages and support actually arrive.

say: I'd ask for **written notice terms** for the six coordinators.
I'd say paid training and **clear support eligibility** must accompany job losses.
think: I expect **both desk wages** to shrink by 2028.
Three weeks of cash would vanish before I found **affordable work**.
do: Ask the **staff representative** for notice and severance terms now.
Postpone the **summer-trip deposit** before paying it.
Apply for **posted goods-receiving work** only after safety training and an affordable wage; check support eligibility.
feel: I feel **alarmed** by two expected income losses and almost no reserve.
S2.quote: Being the best person in this office will not make AGI slower.
fieldNote: His skill cannot protect **thinking procurement** when full AGI arrives.
Goods receiving offers a **short physical bridge**, with schedules exposed in 2028 and lifting in 2031.
He plans to **check eligibility** before seeking public support.

steps.text: Ask staff representative for written notice and severance terms
Postpone summer-trip deposit before paying it
Apply for posted paid receiving work only after safety training and affordable combined wages
Check public support eligibility and apply only if household qualifies

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years could let us pay down a little debt while I still earn, but not if overtime remains frozen forever. Procurement and Leena's library desk still face AGI in 2031. Receiving work is physical for a short stretch, with capable robots around 2034, but its planning and records change in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the company to put paid learning places and their wages in writing. I'd ask our staff representative to negotiate notice time rather than only a farewell payment. I'd tell Leena we should keep the children in the same schools if possible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I could shift into quality inspection on the plant floor if a paid place opens, but my management wage would be hard to match. We need more than a certificate: the mortgage requires monthly cash. Five years gives me a chance, not a guaranteed vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next year I'd ask the quality lead about a paid floor-inspection apprenticeship and complete it only if there is an approved place, safety supervision, shift cover and a wage that keeps our bills paid. I'd put 60 weekly into cash after mortgage and school bills if overtime returns, aiming for three months of expenses. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2031 I'd take a posted inspection role only if its wage with Leena's confirmed pay covers mortgage, food and school costs; otherwise I'd search paid work beyond the district without moving the family on speculation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, not hopeless. A five-year notice gives me time to ask hard questions about a real wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would inspection work involve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd handle returned valves, check seals and photograph damage beside an experienced inspector. The record and decision can be generated in 2031, but a person may still have to turn the metal part until robots arrive around 2034. The inspection floor is not a shelter with a ten-year roof.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if overtime never comes back?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The 60 weekly saving does not happen. We pay the ordinary mortgage and keep the three weeks of cash; I cannot invent a second wage. I'd still ask about paid training, because an unpaid apprenticeship is out of reach.

I'd ask the representative to bargain for **notice time**.
think: A floor inspection place might help, but **pay is uncertain**.
Five years gives us **time to ask**, not a vacancy.

Save **60 weekly** only if overtime resumes and family bills are covered.
Take **posted inspection work** after 2031 only if combined confirmed pay covers bills.
feel: I feel **anxious** about the uncertain inspection wage.
S3.quote: The inspection floor is not a shelter with a ten-year roof.
fieldNote: His proposed inspection shift has **physical handling**, but records face AGI in 2031.
An unpaid apprenticeship is **unaffordable** with only three weeks saved.
Extra saving depends on **overtime returning** and ordinary bills being paid.

steps.text: Complete approved paid floor-inspection apprenticeship only with safety supervision, shift cover and affordable wage
Save 60 weekly only if overtime returns and mortgage and school bills are covered
Take posted inspection job after 2031 only if confirmed combined wages cover family bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2036 I'll be 53, our children twenty and twenty-four. They may have their own paths, but I cannot count their wages for our mortgage. AGI could do procurement and inspection decisions by 2036; capable robots could handle the physical parts around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask our staff representative for a wage path and paid training tied to actual positions. I'd tell my team to document the supplier checks we still own each year. I'd tell Leena we should look at the mortgage balance annually, not guess where the children will live.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A decade may let me rebuild the reserve and reduce debt while I still earn. It does not promise the plant stays open, and the one other local plant may also use AGI. I'd be steadier if we had six months' expenses and a smaller mortgage before 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Beginning this winter I'd ask for a written pay review through our staff representative, naming the overtime freeze and my team's error record. I'd save 75 weekly only after mortgage and school bills if the review restores pay, aiming for six months over time rather than promising a date. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2036, I'd apply for a posted physical inspection job only if trained, supervised and its wage with Leena's confirmed pay covers our bills; if none exists, I'd check support eligibility and ask the lender for terms before arrears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about how long the plant and its pay will last, but ten years gives us room to improve the balance sheet. I cannot treat an imagined new trade as income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your children support you then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I hope they visit and have choices of their own. The younger would be twenty and the older twenty-four; I will not plan to collect rent from them. Our mortgage is ours to manage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why seek a pay review now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The company has used my team's low error rate to renew supplier contracts while our overtime stopped. I want the numbers on the table with a staff representative, not a private favour. A decade is useful only if the wages arrive during it.

I'd tell Leena we must check **mortgage balances annually**.
think: A decade could rebuild **cash and lower debt** while wages continue.
The local plant and its wage are **not guaranteed** until 2036.
do: Seek a **staff-backed pay review** using the team error record this winter.
Save **75 weekly** only if pay rises and family bills are covered.
Apply after 2036 for **posted physical inspection work** only with training and affordable confirmed combined pay.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about the plant's future despite the longer runway.
S4.quote: A decade is useful only if the wages arrive during it.
fieldNote: He refuses to count **adult children's earnings** toward the mortgage.
His long savings target depends on a **real pay rise**, not assumed compounding.
Inspection handling faces **robots around 2039**, while decisions face AGI in 2036.

steps.text: Seek written pay review with staff representative using team error record

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. Both our desk incomes could go before I can rebuild even a month's cash, and my skill in supplier disputes would not change the date. Written notice terms, paid training linked to a real wage and clear support eligibility would help. I would still ask the lender early rather than wait for a missed payment.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who is paying the staff to check the damaged valve after the system has already approved the invoice. The metal part and the computer record can disagree. My children should not have to discover that through an empty account at home.

headlineQuote: The metal part and the computer record can disagree.
portrait: Gareth, **43**, leads six supplier coordinators at a large industrial-parts company and holds an MBA.
He uses AI **daily**, but checks source photographs and is among the strongest managers of supplier disputes.
Low pay, a mortgage, **two school-age children** and three weeks saved leave little room for lost hours.
He seeks **staff-backed terms** and paid work as his thinking-heavy job faces AGI.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove his and Leena's desk incomes before savings recover.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **written notice terms** and paid training linked to a real wage.
He wants **clear support eligibility** and would contact his lender before arrears.
